themes.theme: Costco's distinct shopping experience vs. Amazon
Nintendo's IP monetization and customer data
Ball Corporation's credit rating vs. trading value
Intel's dividend cut and balance sheet issues
BlackBerry's irrelevance in the modern landscape

positions.commentary: The speaker shares an insight from his wife that Amazon and Costco offer different shopping experiences, which saved him money by sticking with Costco after Amazon bought Whole Foods.
The speaker mentions that dismissing a company like Ball out of hand might cause investors to miss opportunities, though he does not own it.
The speaker mentions investing in Amazon in 1997 as an example of a stock that investors can talk about at cocktail parties, contrasting it with boring companies that create shareholder value.
The speaker states that BlackBerry products are not as relevant as they were 20 years ago and are now completely out of the landscape.
The speaker notes that a fund manager holding 50% in Nvidia since the start of the year would be in the top charts, but questions if that is a safe way for a fund manager to allocate.
The speaker mentions Tesla as an example of a 'cocktail party stock' that investors can talk about at cocktail parties, contrasting it with boring companies that create shareholder value.
Intel drew the dividend too much and then had to cut it, which brought problems.

thesis: This episode argues that investors should look beyond surface-level metrics like credit ratings or dividend history to find 'moats' and long-term value, citing examples like Costco's distinct shopping experience and Nintendo's customer data leverage. It suggests that dismissing companies like Ball Corporation or Intel based on their balance sheets or dividend cuts is short-sighted, while also warning against over-allocating to volatile 'cocktail party stocks' like Tesla or Nvidia.

claims.claim: The speaker cites Costco as an example of a company where investors doubted the long-term outlook when Amazon bought Whole Foods, but those with conviction in the terminal state found a great buying opportunity.
claims.quote: So when a stock drops 30%, it might be based on short-term use. But what the market price is applying is that there's a change in how investors you're thinking about the terminal state of this company, so five, 10 years out, what does that look like?

claims.claim: The speaker believes Nintendo management has made slow but steady progress in improving how it thinks about capitalizing or monetizing its intellectual property.
claims.quote: I think Nintendo management has made slow but steady progress in improving how it thinks about capitalizing or monetizing its intellectual property.

claims.claim: The speaker believes that in five, ten years, as new generations of Nintendo IP come out, they will leverage the data they have with customers to create a lifetime relationship.
claims.quote: And I completely believe that in five, ten years, as new generations, the Nintendo IP comes out, they're going to leverage that data that they have with you.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Nintendo has taken advantage of Nintendo accounts, which are personalized sign-ups, and that they have more than 100 million users on the switch.
claims.quote: And you have one thing there, if I'm not mistaken here, it's if you want to play the Switch, you have to create a Nintendo account. Right. So it's not like you can opt in or opt out. It's like you need that. So they have like more than 100 million accounts because they have more than 100 million users on the switch.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that dismissing a company like Ball out of hand for not having an investment grade balance sheet is short-sighted, as it trades like an investment grade despite a double B credit rating.
claims.quote: But I also know some great companies that have double B credit ratings. And their credit trades like an investment grade, like Ball Corporation, which is a packaging company. They make aluminum cans.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that dismissing a company like Ball out of hand might cause investors to miss opportunities, though he does not own it.
claims.quote: And so I think if you dismissed a company like Ball out of hand, which I don't own, but I followed it at Morningstar for three and a half years, I think you might miss some opportunities.

claims.claim: The speaker cites an FT article on Bloomberg's financial information system as a great example of a technology moat that is critical to the financial industry and not likely to be disrupted.
claims.quote: And I thought they did a really nice job kind of breaking the moat of the Bloomberg financial information system and how critical it is to the financial industry. Even though it looks like MS DOS from the 1980s, it's still a critical component of so many investors around the world.

claims.claim: The speaker shares an insight from his wife that Amazon and Costco offer different shopping experiences, which saved him money by sticking with Costco after Amazon bought Whole Foods.
claims.quote: And my bride went home to my wife and I asked, is this, should I be, should I be concerned about this? And she goes, no, they're different different shopping experiences. And so that was a great, great insight that saved and made me a lot of money over time with sticking with Costco and thanks to my wife.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that there was concern among Costco members or investors that Amazon buying Whole Foods would lead to Amazon delivering everything to your door, but he considers the experiences different.
claims.quote: I remember when Amazon bought Whole Foods in the U.S., there was a lot of concern among Costco members or Costco investors that, oh, here we go. Amazon's going to deliver everything to your door. No one's going to need to go to Costco anymore.

claims.quote: I mean, Kodaks recognizable and and BlackBerry is recognizable, but their products are not as relevant as relevant as they were 20 years ago. claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Kodak is recognizable but their products are not as relevant as they were 20 years ago.
claims.quote: I mean, Kodaks recognizable and and BlackBerry is recognizable, but their products are not as relevant as relevant as they were 20 years ago.

claims.quote: I think the example you mentioned is a good one because if you, if you look at Bloomberg's UX and that it continues to grow, then that's for me, for me, it's a sign of a mode. Because if with that with that ux, people are not switching out, then obviously there's something more than just technology.

claims.quote: But I don't know if that's a safe way, not for maybe you as a fund manager, but you also have to think on the people that are behind your money. Because maybe you can be comfortable with that, but maybe the person that's giving you their money is not so comfortable with that.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions holding Amazon since 1999 as an example of a company that made shareholders super rich, noting that few people endured the 90% drop.
claims.quote: So let's say you held Amazon Amazon since it's 1999. Well, obviously, you are super rich now. But how many people endure that 90% drop? I mean, probably less than 5% of the shareholders. And I'm being very generous, probably.

claims.quote: And then in luxury, he owns LVMH and Hermes. And obviously, that made me believe that he was a top-down, he followed a top-down approach, but then he told me that that's not true because he is bottom.
